citation.title: How foes become allies: the shifting role of business in climate politics
citation.venue_or_publisher: Policy Sciences 57, 101-124 (2024), per the page's 'Cite this article' line; published online 16 November 2023; issue date March 2024

question: Under what conditions firms shift from opposing to supporting costly policy reform; develops a dynamic theory of change in business policy positions (opposition, strategic support, sincere support) and applies it to US climate politics. It does not ask how large business or fossil-fuel presence is in any forum.
data: Mainly published research on business lobbying in US climate politics (academic articles and reports), plus the authors' own primary research where published work was scarce: newspaper articles (keyword search in Factiva, national and subnational papers), Congressional hearings and position papers. Three sectors (electric utilities, oil and gas, automakers) in the USA over three periods, mid-1990s to 2020. Firm-level figures (coal share of generation, lobbying spend, fleet fuel economy) are taken from cited secondary sources.
method: Conceptual theory building followed by a qualitative historical case analysis. A firm's material interest is judged from its assets (generation mix, fuel mix, fleet fuel economy); if the stated position matches that interest it is coded sincere, if it does not match, strategic. Consistency of positions across political venues is used as a second check. No statistical or language-model classification.

definitions.definition: Material interests closely linked to profitability; they shape how firms rank policy alternatives.
definitions.quote: In the case of firms, interests are primarily material and closely linked to profitability, shaping how firms rank the desirability of different policy alternatives

definitions.definition: Expressed opposition or support for a policy in a given political environment.
definitions.quote: we define policy positions as expressed opposition or support for a policy in a given political environment.

definitions.definition: Sincere: an expressed first-order preference aligned with material interests. Strategic: an expressed second-order or lower-ranked preference misaligned with economic interests.
definitions.quote: We define a sincere position as an expressed first-order preference aligned with material interests, and a strategic position as an expressed, second-order or lower-ranked preference misaligned with economic interests.

definitions.definition: The text does not define 'business' in general. It analyses individual firms in three named sectors and the industry associations they belong to.
No definition. The sectors are chosen as major emitters of greenhouse gases; individual firms are described by the share of coal, oil or gas in their assets.
definitions.quote: Our analysis focuses on the major contributors to the emission of greenhouse gases (GHGs), including electric utilities, oil and gas firms, and automakers

proxies.concept: Firm interest of an electric utility
proxies.indicator: Cleanness and carbon intensity of its power generation portfolio (for example share of coal, nuclear, hydropower, gas).
proxies.quote: For electric utilities, we assess the relative cleanness and carbon intensity of their power generation portfolios.

proxies.concept: Firm interest of an oil and gas company
proxies.indicator: Carbon intensity of its fuel portfolio and its interest in growing natural gas production.
proxies.quote: For oil and gas firms, we examine the relative carbon intensity of their fuel portfolios and consider interests tied to of growth natural gas production.

proxies.indicator: Whether the deduced interest matches the observed support or opposition; plus whether the position stays the same across political venues.
proxies.quote: If the deduced interest of firms align with observed support or opposition to the reform in question, we assume that the firm's policy position is sincere, reflecting a first-order preference.

proxies.concept: Sectors expected to resist climate policy
proxies.indicator: Sector membership (electric utilities, oil and gas, automakers), justified by their share of climate-related lobbying spending and high emissions.
proxies.quote: Together, they accounted for at least 56 percent of climate-related lobbying expenditures in the USA between 2000 and 2016 (Brulle, 2018).

proxies.indicator: Share of coal in its generation portfolio, from cited benchmarking reports.
proxies.quote: The AEP had 84 percent and Duke nearly 70 percent coal in their generation portfolios (Atten, Curry, & Saha, 2008).

proxies.concept: Effort a firm puts into opposing or supporting climate policy
proxies.indicator: Climate lobbying expenditure in US dollars, taken from cited studies.
proxies.quote: ExxonMobil, the absolute largest US emitter, spent USD 27.4 million on lobbying in 2008

findings.claim: In the cap-and-trade period, many emitting utilities and oil and gas firms moved from opposition to strategic support, driven by political pressure.
findings.quote: a considerable share of electric utilities and oil and gas firms shifted from opposition to strategic support for a favorably designed cap-and-trade scheme

findings.claim: Support by these firms was judged strategic partly because they stayed in industry associations that worked against the legislation.
findings.quote: This rent-seeking and inconsistencies in positioning across venues further point to their support being strategic.

findings.claim: In the 1990s, major utilities, oil and gas firms, automakers and their branch organisations organised together against climate policy.
findings.quote: Members of the GCC included all the leading firms and branch organizations
findings.page: Phase 1: industry unity and opposition to climate policy

findings.claim: In the Clean Power Plan period, most broad-based industry associations and coal-intensive firms continued to oppose the rule.
findings.quote: So did most of the broad-based industry associations, including the CoC and the NAM.

findings.claim: Oil and gas majors' later support for a carbon tax was judged partly sincere and partly strategic.
findings.quote: which suggests that the policy positions of oil and gas majors may have been partly strategic and partly sincere.
findings.page: Regulatory rollbacks under the trump administration

findings.claim: Authors conclude that political pressure produces only strategic support, while policy and market change are more likely to produce sincere support.
findings.quote: whereas political mechanisms are likely to result in only strategic support for reform, policy and market change are more likely to drive sincere policy support.

limitations.point: The text file holds the full running text, notes and reference list. The four tables (relationship of interests, conditions, drivers, cases) are given only as captions; their contents are not in the file, so nothing is recorded from them.
Inferring a firm's real preference from its stated position is hard, and the authors say their analysis still faces this problem.
limitations.quote: the empirical analysis is still subject to the “problem of preferences” that presents a challenge to all firm-centered analyses of politics

limitations.point: Interests are judged from secondary assessments, which the authors accept because the article is a historical overview.
limitations.quote: The use of secondary assessments is appropriate for this article, given our goal to provide a historical overview of the evolution of firm positions.

limitations.point: Evidence comes from one country only, chosen as a hard test, so it does not speak to delegations at UN climate talks.
limitations.quote: We probe the plausibility of our theory in the case of the USA.

limitations.point: Part of the analysis is a review of other studies rather than new data, with the authors' own research only where published work is scarce.
limitations.quote: Our empirical analysis of shifts in business positioning is written partly as a review article
